GTI

Create an interactive Great Tables object.

Usage

Source

GTI(
    data,
    rowname_col=None,
    groupname_col=None,
    auto_align=True,
    id=None,
    locale=None,
    preset="report",
    order_by=None,
)

The GTI() class makes a table that readers can work with in the browser: they can sort it by its columns, search it, page through it, resize its columns, and (if allowed) select its rows. It’s a GT table in every other way, so all of GT’s methods (formatting, styling, spanners, summary rows, and the rest) can be used to make it. What readers can do with it is set by the methods beginning with i_ (e.g., i_pagination() or i_search()), which only GTI tables have.

A GTI table is always rendered as interactive HTML: the table’s own HTML, made as for a GT table, inside a <gt-table> element that adds the controls. The element needs no other libraries, and the table can be read before (or without) its script running. A GTI table can’t be saved as an image or a PDF, or rendered as LaTeX; for those, use a GT table.

To make a published GT table browsable (sortable, searchable, filterable, and paged), with the options R gt has for that, opt_interactive() may be all that’s needed; it renders the table with the same engine. GTI is for a table that’s an interface, one readers work with, and GTI.from_gt() turns a GT table into one.

A table of a lazy frame (a Polars LazyFrame, a DuckDB relation or an Ibis table) is made, formatted and styled as any other, but its rows are collected only as they’re shown. Shown as a widget (with i_as_widget()) or in a Shiny app (with render_gt()), a table of more rows than the browser is quick with keeps them in Python (see i_scale()): each view is found with a query on the frame, and only the rows of the page shown are collected, formatted and rendered. Anywhere else (or with few rows), all the rows are collected and the table is shown as a table of them would be.

The table is made again from the rows shown, by the same methods: so what depends on every row can’t be used (data_color(), a footnote on the body or the stub, or rows chosen by their positions, rather than by an expression or their names in the stub); and a method that looks at the rows it’s given looks only at the page’s (as an expression of a column’s mean does, in tab_style()‘s rows, or cols_align_decimal(), or a nanoplot’s scale). A table with summary rows or row groups has all its rows collected. In Python, its search, and its filters’ “contains” and “matches” clauses, match the rows’ values as text (e.g., 1000.5), not the text of their cells (1,000.50), and a missing value matches nothing.

A DuckDB relation’s or an Ibis table’s rows have no order that’s kept from one query to the next, so they’re shown in the order of their values: sorted by the columns of order_by=, then by every other column (but those of lists, structs and objects). A Polars LazyFrame’s are in its own order, unless it’s given an order_by=. The collected rows, and their data (as the widget’s view() gives it), are of the frame’s backend: a Polars DataFrame, for a LazyFrame, and a PyArrow table, for DuckDB and Ibis.

Warning

GTI() is experimental: its methods, and what they do, may change.

Parameters

data: Any

A DataFrame object, or a lazy frame: a Polars LazyFrame, a DuckDB relation or an Ibis table (whose rows are collected as they’re shown: see above).

rowname_col: str | list[str] | None = None

The column name in the input data= table to use as row labels to be placed in the table stub. A list of column names creates a hierarchical stub.

groupname_col: str | None = None

The column name in the input data= table to use as group labels for generation of row groups.

auto_align: bool = True

Optionally have column data be aligned depending on the content contained in each column of the input data=.

id: str | None = None

By default (with None) the table ID will be a random, ten-letter string as generated through internal use of the random_id() function. A custom table ID can be used here by providing a string.

locale: str | None = None

An optional locale identifier that can be set as the default locale for all functions that take a locale argument.

preset: Preset = "report"

The settings the table starts with: "report" (the default) for a table to be read, with the controls above; or "explorer" for a look through data, as if made with i_cols_filter() and i_cols_profile() (every column filtered and profiled, as its kind suggests), i_cols_controls(hideable=True, reorderable=True) (every column can be hidden and moved), i_display(compact=True, wrap=False, monospace=True) (compact rows of one line each, in a monospaced font), i_export("csv") and i_inspect() (row numbers, dtypes under the labels, what the data is and its number of rows and columns, and missing values tinted). The stub is left out of these, as those methods leave it out. The i_ methods change a preset as they change any table: each sets all of its feature’s settings (so i_display(wrap=True) on an explorer lets its text wrap, but also makes its rows less compact and puts them in the table’s own font, unless it’s given compact=True and monospace=True too), and the i_cols_ methods set those of the columns they’re given.

order_by: str | list[str] | None = None
For a lazy frame, the columns its rows are in the order of (and numbered by): the rows sort by them first, then by the frame’s other columns (see above). A column of unique values (an ID) is best, which leaves them nothing to sort. Not for a DataFrame (which can be sorted first, for the table).

Returns

GTI
A GTI object is returned.

Examples

Out of the box, a GTI table can be sorted by its columns (with the arrows under their labels), searched, and paged through, ten rows at a time, and its columns can be resized.

from great_tables import GTI
from great_tables.data import towny

towny_mini = towny[["name", "status", "csd_type", "population_2021"]]

GTI(towny_mini, rowname_col="name").fmt_integer(columns="population_2021")

With preset="explorer", the table is set up for looking through data: each column can be filtered (from the button by its label) and has a profile of its values, with its dtype, the rows are numbered, compact and monospaced, missing values are tinted, the status line above the table says what the data is and how much of it there is, and the rows can be downloaded.

from great_tables.data import gtcars

GTI(gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp", "ctry_origin"]], preset="explorer")

A GT table can be made into a GTI table with GTI.from_gt().

A table of a Polars LazyFrame keeps its rows there until they’re shown.

import polars as pl
from great_tables import GTI

lf = pl.scan_parquet("trips.parquet")

GTI(lf).fmt_number(columns="fare", decimals=2).i_cols_filter("payment").i_as_widget()

And so does a table of a DuckDB relation, in DuckDB, its rows in the order of a column of IDs.

import duckdb

trips = duckdb.read_parquet("trips.parquet")

GTI(trips, order_by="trip_id").i_cols_filter("payment").i_as_widget()
